newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters, UPS remain far apart as strike deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters, UPS remain far apart as strike deadline looms.

text.p: The Teamsters union and United Parcel Service of America Inc. remained far apart Thursday ahead of a midnight strike deadline after the union rejected what the nation's largest package delivery firm said was its final offer.

A strike would affect almost 200,000 unionized workers -- about two-thirds of the UPS work force -- and could halt package deliveries for consumers and companies across America. UPS delivers 12 million packages a day.

Earlier Thursday, Ken Hall, co-chairman of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters' negotiating committee, said the UPS offer failed to address key issues, including an end to subcontracting, more full-time jobs, wages, pensions and health and safety issues.

"UPS claims to have made a final offer," Hall said. "The fact is the last offer that UPS has put on the table does not address all the serious issues and the serious proposals that we have put on the table."
But Hall, speaking from Washington, said the union remained willing to negotiate.
Asked if a strike could still be avoided, he said: "Absolutely, if the company comes to the table and negotiates seriously, we can reach agreement before midnight."
UPS spokesman Ken Sternad called the union leadership "awfully misguided."
"I can confirm that it is not our intention to make substantive changes to this final and best offer," he said in a conference call with reporters.

"To say it couldn't be noodled here or a penny couldn't be changed there ... certainly doesn't do us any good in trying to reach a final accommodation with the union. We're willing to hear what they have to say about it, but this is the best offer we're going to make in terms of the totality of it."
A senior White House aide met with officials from both UPS and the union, but a spokesman for President Clinton declined to say whether the administration would intervene in the labour dispute.
"I'm not going to speculate on that at this point, we've just had contact with the parties to understand better their deliberations," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

UPS said its offer would increase pay for both full- and part-time workers by $1.50 to $2.50 per hour over five years. It said it would also guarantee that no UPS driver is replaced or eliminated through subcontracting.
The company's contract with the Teamsters expires at midnight EDT (0400 GMT). UPS has said it cannot promise it will be able to complete deliveries beyond Thursday.
"We wouldn't be able to continue to accept anywhere near our daily volume. There's no question we couldn't do that," Sternad said.

"But some of our higher premium and international services, obviously we would look to every way to perhaps provide service on those packages, although again, there would come a juncture where with a complete shutdown that wouldn't be possible."

The company said its new offer proposes a restructuring of UPS pension benefits. It said the offer, made Wednesday, includes a wage and benefits package that would keep UPS Teamsters the highest-paid workers in the industry.

The company said it would agree to provide 10,000 opportunities for part-time employees to move into full-time jobs over the life of the agreement. It would also create 1,000 new full-time jobs from part-time jobs.

The company said the pension restructuring it has proposed would increase monthly benefits for full- and part-time employees by an average of 50 percent. Retirees would be covered under new pension plans created outside the Teamsters' multi-employer pension system, it said.
"We recognise that it is difficult for the union leadership to accept this new pension plan," Sternad said earlier.
UPS said its proposal is "a fair and generous offer that addresses all key points raised by the union during negotiations."
The Teamsters represent about two-thirds of the company's domestic payroll, including delivery truck drivers, tractor-trailer drivers and package facility workers.
